meta.name: 墨语
meta.description: Minimal pairs deck — characters that look or sound similar, drilled back-to-back so ear and hand learn to tell them apart.

pronunciationRules.description: Tongue tip flat, just behind lower front teeth. Like a relaxed smile 😊.
Tongue tip curled back toward the roof of the mouth 🤫. Feels like whispering 'shhh'.

errorMap.pattern: z- vs sh-, same -uo vowel
errorMap.note: Flat vs curled tongue. Card 001 — active.

errorMap.pattern: x- vs sh-, same -ang vowel
errorMap.note: x- is blade-palatal (front of mouth); sh- is retroflex (curled back). Planned.

errorMap.pattern: -uo vs -u, same sh- initial
errorMap.note: Vowel distinction. Planned.

errorMap.pattern: n- initial unclear
errorMap.note: n- vs l- confusion, or n- dropping entirely. Planned.

errorMap.pattern: nǚ vs nǐ vowel, fast-speech compression of shénme → sme
errorMap.note: 女/你 tone-3 vowel confusion; 什么 elision in natural speech. Card 002 — active.

errorMap.pattern: z- (flat) vs n- (nasal tap) vs sh- (retroflex) — all 1-syllable function words
errorMap.note: 在→那→是 are speech recognition's worst nightmare. Card 003 — active.

errorMap.pattern: perfect homophones — same sound tíng, different tone
errorMap.note: 听 (tīng, 1st) vs 庭 (tíng, 2nd) — app picks wrong char when tone is off. Card 003.

errorMap.pattern: n- nasal tap vs q- (ch sound), tone 3 (dipping) vs tone 4 (falling)
errorMap.note: 哪 (which/where) + common traps with 听 (listening vs 庭 temple). Card 004 — active.

errorMap.pattern: Listening comprehension trap: 著 (zhe, light particle) vs 他 (tā, he)
errorMap.note: 聽著說 (listened to speaking) vs 听他说 (listen to him speak) — same tone pattern, different consonants. Card 004.

errorMap.pattern: visual trap: 口 shape in 兑 (wide/short) vs 口 in 斿 (tall/narrow)
errorMap.note: 说 has 讠(speech) + 兑 with SQUATTING 口. 游 has 氵(water) + 斿 with STRETCHING 口. Same mouth radical, different outfit. Card 005 — active.

errorMap.pattern: perfect homophones — both zài (tone 4), only context separates them
errorMap.note: 在 (at/now/existing) vs 再 (again/repeat). 你在听我说吗 vs 你再听我说吗 — ear cannot distinguish. Card 005.

errorMap.pattern: visual radical contrast: 亻(person) vs 氵(water)
errorMap.note: 们 (plural suffix; neutral tone) vs 淇 (loan-sound in 冰淇淋). Card 006 — active.

errorMap.pattern: huí vs huì tone contour + mouth closure timing
errorMap.note: Learner says huí when intending huì; lips stay open instead of closing at the end. Card 006 trap.

errorMap.pattern: zh- retroflex vs z- flat-tongue swap
errorMap.note: Tongue remained flat for 做 (zuò) when it should contrast with curled zh- in 周. Card 006 trap.

errorMap.pattern: partial match + lexical autocorrect from shénme
errorMap.note: Brain latched onto initial sh- and guessed the remainder under speed/noise. Card 006 trap.

errorMap.pattern: x- palatal + -iang glide vs b- stop + -u
errorMap.note: Core contrast for Card 007: miss/think vs NOT, with strong tone contrast (3rd vs 4th).

errorMap.pattern: -iang glide vs -eng openness
errorMap.note: Learner confuses xiǎng and shēng under speed; fix by exaggerating the i-glide in 想.

errorMap.pattern: same -uo rhyme, tone 1 flat vs tone 4 falling
errorMap.note: High-frequency trap surfaced again in Card 007 sentence drills.

errorMap.pattern: identical sound (nǎlǐ) — Simplified 里 vs Traditional 裡, script difference only
errorMap.note: Both correct. 裡 is the Traditional form (Taiwan/HK) for 'inside'; 里 is Simplified. Card 008 — active.

errorMap.pattern: n- tongue-tip (你) vs w- lip-rounding (我), same tone-3 dip-rise shape
errorMap.note: 你 nǐ = tongue tip behind teeth, air flows out; 我 wǒ = lips round into 'o' then open. Card 008 — active.

errorMap.pattern: ɕ- flat tongue/spread lips (想) vs ʂ- curled tongue/rounded lips (上), same -ang rhyme and both falling/dipping tones
errorMap.note: Cheat code: 心 (heart) at the bottom of 想 = feeling/desire; 上 is a pure direction pictograph with no 心. Card 009 — active.

errorMap.pattern: perfect homophones tā (1st tone) — only the written radical (亻 vs 女) differs
errorMap.note: 她 was invented in 1920 by 刘半农, swapping 亻 for 女 to create a dedicated female pronoun. Card 010 — active.

errorMap.pattern: no phonetic similarity (chī vs qù) — lexical perseveration, not a sound confusion
errorMap.note: 吃 gets dropped and 去 gets doubled when 去 already appears earlier in the sentence — the brain reuses the word already in play. Card 009/010 bonus trap.

errorMap.pattern: same 4th-tone contour, high-frequency function-word collision
errorMap.note: Core contrast for Card 011: 不 (ongoing/future negation) vs 是 (to be/correct).

errorMap.pattern: tone collapse in fast speech: 2+2 vs 3+3
errorMap.note: 拿来 ná lái and 哪里 nǎlǐ flatten toward the same na-li shape under speed; train tone contour + final vowel spread.

errorMap.pattern: perfect homophones gōng (tone 1), meaning split only by context and writing
errorMap.note: 工 = work/craft (I-beam shape) vs 公 = public/fair. Card 012 — active.

errorMap.pattern: perfect homophones zài (tone 4), location vs repetition
errorMap.note: 在 = location/presence vs 再 = again/repeat. Core trap in 你在哪里工作. Card 012.

errorMap.pattern: lexical substitution under pressure (ch- vs q-, no true phonetic overlap)
errorMap.note: 吃 can be replaced by 去 when 去 already appears earlier in sentence planning. Card 012.

errorMap.pattern: perfect homophones tā (tone 1), radical-only written contrast
errorMap.note: Speech must rely on context; writing disambiguates with 亻 vs 女. Card 012 reinforcement.

homework.task: Forvo × 5 each: forvo.com/word/做/ and forvo.com/word/说/
Hanzi Flow writing session × 3 each
Tongue drill: alternate 做-说 10×
Record yourself: 我会做，不会说。 (Wǒ huì zuò, bù huì shuō.)
Forvo × 5 each: forvo.com/word/他/ and forvo.com/word/什么/
Lip drill: 女 (round lips) vs 你 (spread lips) — alternate 10×
Record yourself: 你做什么工作？她做什么工作？他们在说什么？
Forvo × 5 each: forvo.com/word/哪/ and forvo.com/word/去/
Hanzi Flow writing session × 3 each
Tone drill: 哪 (3rd dipping ↙↗) vs 去 (4th falling ↘)
Record yourself: 你在听我说吗？你去哪里？ (Are you listening to me? Where are you going?)
Forvo × 5: forvo.com/word/听/ (listen — 1st tone HIGH FLAT)
Consonant trap: 聽著說 vs 听他说 (著 zhe vs 他 tā) — say 10× each
Forvo × 5 each: forvo.com/word/说/#zh and forvo.com/word/游/#zh
Visual drill: draw 口 inside 兑 (WIDE/SHORT) and inside 斿 (TALL/NARROW) — say aloud the difference
Tongue drill: 说 (sh- curled) vs 游 (y- glide) — alternate 10×
Record yourself: 你在听我说吗？你喜欢游泳吗？(Are you listening? Do you like swimming?)
Listening trap drill: 你在(zài)听我说吗 vs 你再(zài)听我说吗 — can you hear the difference? (You cannot — use context!)
Forvo × 5 each: forvo.com/word/们 and forvo.com/word/淇
Mouth drill: 会(huì) lips CLOSE at the end; compare with 回(huí) lips stay more open
Contrast drill 10×: 什么(shénme) vs 生亡(shēngwáng) — keep -en relaxed, avoid -eng pull
Record yourself: 我们今天吃冰淇淋！你会做什么工作？他们在说什么？
Forvo × 5 each: forvo.com/word/想 and forvo.com/word/不
Contrast drill: 想 xiǎng (i-glide + 3rd tone dip-rise) vs 生 shēng (open vowel + flat 1st tone) — 10×
Initial drill: 怎么 zěnme vs 人们 rénmen — z- teeth contact vs r- tongue curl, keep same -nme ending
Record yourself: 你想我了，不是你生完了！他不会做，不是他不会说！
Forvo × 5 each: forvo.com/word/里/ and forvo.com/word/法/
Hanzi Flow writing session × 3 each — focus on the central 丨 spine in 里 and the flowing 氵 three dots in 法
Tongue drill: 你 nǐ (tongue tip, n-) vs 我 wǒ (lip-round, w-) — alternate 10×
Record yourself: 你在哪里工作？我会做什么？这个方法不合法。
Forvo × 5 each: forvo.com/word/想/ and forvo.com/word/上/
Lip drill: 想 xiǎng (lips SPREAD, tongue flat — 'shee-AHNG') vs 上 shàng (lips ROUND, tongue curled back — 'shrr-AHNG') — alternate 10×
Hanzi Flow writing session × 3 each — focus on the 3 dots in 心 (想) flowing left→right→center, and the long bottom 一 stroke in 上 staying perfectly horizontal
Forvo × 5 each: forvo.com/word/他/, forvo.com/word/她/, forvo.com/word/吃/, and forvo.com/word/去/
Radical-recall drill: 他 (亻person) vs 她 (女woman) — say each aloud, then write the radical that disambiguates it, 10×
Record yourself: 我想去哪里吃，不是我上去哪里去！她是哪里的人？
Forvo × 5 each: forvo.com/word/不/ and forvo.com/word/是/
Tone drill: 不 bù (short clipped 4th tone) vs 是 shì (quick retroflex 4th tone) — alternate 10×
Contrast drill: 不 = ongoing/future negation; 没 = completed past negation. Say paired examples 5× each.
Record yourself: 我不是神，你想去哪里？你去拿来！

pairs.title: 工 vs 在
pairs.subtitle: work/craft vs at/in/existing
pairs.prompt: 哪个是 work？哪个是 at？
pairs.promptEn: Which one means work? Which one means at/in?

trapZone.confusion: 尼索遜馬公索 → 你做什么工作？; 你再拿給他們做 → 你在哪里工作？; 他不是哪里的人 → 她是哪里的人？; 我們上去哪裡去 → 你想去哪里吃？
trapZone.reason: 在 and 再 are perfect homophones (zài, tone 4), so only context separates location from repetition. 工 and 公 are also perfect homophones (gōng, tone 1), so writing context must carry meaning. Additional trap chains come from lexical carry-over and tone flattening in fast speech: 吃 can be replaced by 去 when 去 is already active in planning, and 他/她 cannot be distinguished by sound alone.

drill.en: Where do you want to eat?

characters.pronunciation: goong (hold the vowel flat; lips gently rounded at the end)
characters.calligraphy: NARROW ║ WIDE balance. Keep the middle horizontal stroke perfectly centered between the top and bottom lines.
characters.culture: 工匠 (gōngjiàng) means artisan/craftsman. In the old four-class model 士农工商, craftsmen were ranked last: scholars > farmers > merchants > craftsmen.
characters.etymology: A very old pictograph linked to tools and measured straightness (often taught via the carpenter's square). The three horizontals plus central connector became a stable 'I-beam' shape: beam, support, and connection. From tool-making and craft activity, the meaning generalized to work/labor.

characters.english: at / in / existing / to be present
characters.pronunciation: dzai (front tongue contact, then a fast drop)
characters.calligraphy: TALL ║ SHORT balance. Keep the left 土 upright and stable as the ground anchor.
characters.culture: 正在 (zhèngzài) marks ongoing action in modern Mandarin (progressive '-ing'): 我正在吃 = 'I am eating right now'.
characters.etymology: Common teaching breakdown: 土 (earth/ground) + 才 (sprouting form). A sprout existing on the ground became the image of presence at a location, then generalized to 'to be at/in' and grammatical progressive marking.

pairs.title: 不 vs 是
pairs.subtitle: not (ongoing/future) vs is/correct
pairs.promptEn: Which one is 不 (not)? Which one is 是 (is/correct)?

trapZone.confusion: 你上去哪里? → 你想去哪里？; 你去哪裡? → 你去拿來!
trapZone.reason: 想 xiǎng (3rd tone) and 上 shàng (4th tone) often collapse in fast speech when the -iang/-ang contrast is reduced. 拿来 ná lái (2nd+2nd) and 哪里 nǎlǐ (3rd+3rd) can both flatten toward na-li in casual speech, so context and tone contour must carry the distinction.

drill.en: Where do you want to go?
Go get it and bring it here!

characters.pronunciation: boo (short and clipped; do not hold the vowel)
characters.calligraphy: TALL ║ SHORT balance. Keep the top horizontal line stable, and let the vertical/downward motion cut cleanly through the center.
characters.culture: 不 is not just a blunt 'no' in Mandarin usage. It is the default negator for ongoing, habitual, or future actions (我不去), while 没 marks completed negation (我没去).
characters.etymology: Radical story: 一 (ground line) + 卜 (sprout). A sprout presses upward but has not yet fully broken through the ground: 尚未. From this 'not yet fulfilled' image came the core negation meaning 'not'.

characters.pronunciation: shr (quick retroflex sh-, tongue curled back)
characters.calligraphy: WIDE ║ NARROW balance. Keep 日 centered above 止 so the top sits square and the lower strokes remain grounded.
characters.culture: 是 began with the sense of 'that is right/correct' and later grammaticalized into the copular verb 'to be' in modern Mandarin.
characters.etymology: Radical story: 日 (sun/truth) + 止 (foot/step). The image is walking toward what is true and correct; from 'correct' it extended to 'this is...'.

pairs.title: 他 vs 她
pairs.subtitle: he vs she — perfect homophones, radical is the only clue
pairs.promptEn: Which is 他 (he)? Which is 她 (she)?

trapZone.confusion: 他是哪里的人？ → 她是哪里的人？ (他→她, identical sound); 你上去哪里去？ → 你想去哪里吃？ (吃 dropped, 去 doubled)
trapZone.reason: 他 and 她 are perfect homophones — tā, 1st tone, identical in speech. The ONLY difference is the written radical: 亻(person, generic/male) vs 女(woman). Before 1920 there was no 她 at all — 刘半农 created it by swapping the radical, so context (or the written word) is the only way to tell them apart. Bonus trap: 吃 chī (mouth radical 口, 'to eat') and 去 qù ('to go', a pictograph of a person leaving a doorway) sound nothing alike, but if 去 already appears earlier in a sentence the brain often reuses it and drops 吃 entirely.

drill.en: Where does he want to go eat?

drill.zh: 我想去哪里吃，不是我上去哪里去！
drill.py: Wǒ xiǎng qù nǎlǐ chī, bùshì wǒ shàngqù nǎlǐ qù!
drill.en: I want to go eat somewhere, not go up somewhere!

characters.pronunciation: tah (flat, like a doctor saying 'open and say ahh')
characters.calligraphy: Left 亻 is TALL and THIN (standing person). Right 也 is WIDE with a sweeping hook. NARROW ║ WIDE — a person reaching toward someone else.
characters.culture: Before the 1920s, 他 was used for everyone — men, women, even objects. In classical texts, 他 could be anyone; context was everything.
characters.etymology: Radical breakdown: 亻(person) + 也 (also/too) — 'that person, too'. 也 supplies the sound (tā); 亻 supplies the generic 'person' meaning.

characters.pronunciation: tah (identical sound to 他 — only the written radical differs)
characters.calligraphy: Left 女 (woman) is TALL with a graceful curve. Right 也 is WIDE with a sweeping hook. NARROW ║ WIDE — same skeleton as 他, different left radical.
characters.culture: 她 was invented in 1920 by 刘半农 (Liú Bànnóng), who swapped 亻(person) for 女(woman) to create a dedicated female pronoun — one of the most influential single-character reforms in modern Chinese.
characters.etymology: Radical breakdown: 女 (woman, semantic) + 也 (phonetic, tā). Identical sound to 他 — 也 supplies the sound in both characters; only the left radical (亻 vs 女) carries the meaning, and you cannot hear that difference.

pairs.title: 想 vs 上
pairs.subtitle: to want/think vs up/to go up
pairs.prompt: 哪个是想要？哪个是上去？
pairs.promptEn: Which one means 'want'? Which one means 'go up'?

trapZone.confusion: 你上去哪里？ → 你想去哪里吃？ (想→上, 吃 dropped); 你上去哪里去？ → 你想去哪里吃？ (doubled 去)
trapZone.reason: 想 xiǎng and 上 shàng share the -ang rhyme, and both tones dip or fall, so the brain hears '___-ang' either way. The real difference is the initial: 想 starts with ɕ (tongue flat behind the lower teeth, lips spread — 'shee'); 上 starts with ʂ (tongue curled back, lips rounded — 'shr'). Cheat code: 心 (heart) at the bottom of 想 = FEELING/desire; 上 = pure direction, no heart. 吃 chī (mouth radical 口, eating) and 去 qù (a person leaving a doorway) sound nothing alike — but once 去 is already in the sentence, the brain panic-fills with it again and drops 吃.

drill.en: Where do I want to go eat?
Where am I going up to?

characters.english: to want / to think of / to miss
characters.pronunciation: /ɕjɑŋ/ — 'shee-AHNG', tongue flat behind lower teeth, lips spread
characters.calligraphy: TALL ║ SHORT. 心 (heart) sits wide at the bottom — it anchors the character. Focus stroke: the 3 dots in 心 must flow left → right → center, not random.
characters.culture: 想 is the #1 verb for desires: 我想你 (I miss you, literally 'I want you'), 想家 (miss home, literally 'want-home').
characters.etymology: Radical breakdown: 相 (木 tree + 目 eye = 'appearance / look carefully') + 心 (heart) at the bottom. ~3000 years ago: 'to look into your heart' = to think, to desire, to want. What appears IN your heart = what you WANT.

characters.english: up / above / to go up / to attend
characters.pronunciation: /ʂɑŋ/ — 'SHR-AHNG', tongue curled back, lips rounded
characters.calligraphy: SHORT ║ TALL. The top 一 is short, the bottom 一 is long — the long bottom line must be perfectly horizontal, like a floor.
characters.culture: 上 also means 'to attend': 上学 (go up to school = attend school), 上班 (go up to work = go to work).
characters.etymology: Pure pictograph — a short line above a long line = 'the thing above'. One of the oldest characters in Chinese; no radical to decompose, it IS the radical. 上去 = go up, 上楼 = go upstairs.

pairs.title: 里 vs 法
pairs.subtitle: inside/village vs law/method/Dharma
pairs.promptEn: Which is lǐ? Which is fǎ?

trapZone.confusion: 你在哪裡 → 你在哪里; 你去哪裡 → 你去哪里; 你想去哪裡 → 你想去哪里; 你做了的什麼 → 我会做什么
trapZone.reason: 里 vs 裡 — same sound, different character. Both are correct: 里 is Simplified (mainland China), 裡 is Traditional (Taiwan/HK) — not an error, just a script habit. 你 vs 我 — same tone-3 dip-rise shape but different starting sound: 你 nǐ = tongue tip behind teeth, air flows out (n-); 我 wǒ = lips round into 'o' then open (w-). 做什么 vs 做了的什麼 — fast speech (快嘴) blurs 什么 (shénme) into something that sounds like 了 (le).

characters.pronunciation: lee (rhymes with 'knee', but the tone dips low then rises)
characters.calligraphy: TALL ║ NARROW. Focus on the central vertical stroke (丨) that pierces through 田 and 土 — it's the spine of the character.
characters.culture: 一里 ≈ 500 metres — ancient China measured distance in 里. 十里 = 5km, roughly an afternoon's walk to the next village.
characters.etymology: Radical breakdown: 田 (field, top) + 土 (earth, bottom). 3000+ years ago a 里 was a village unit — families living inside measured field plots bounded by earthen borders. 'Inside the walls' → village → neighbourhood → (later) 'inside'.

characters.pronunciation: faa (like 'far' but shorter, with the tone dipping then rising)
characters.calligraphy: WIDE ║ SHORT, balanced. Focus on the 氵 three dots — they should flow like water droplets, not sit as static dots.
characters.culture: In Buddhism 法 = Dharma (佛法) — this single character carries the entire concept of universal cosmic law. One of the most important characters in Chinese philosophy: law, method, truth, all in one.
characters.etymology: Radical breakdown: 氵(water, left) + 去 (go/remove, right). Originally meant 'to wash away' — water removing impurities. 氵= cleansing, 去 = remove the impure, leaving what is pure and standard → STANDARD → RULE → LAW.

pairs.title: 想 vs 不
pairs.subtitle: to miss/think vs not
pairs.prompt: 哪个是 miss？哪个是 not？
pairs.promptEn: Which one means miss/think? Which one means not?

trapZone.confusion: 你生完了？ → 你想我了？; 人们啦 → 怎么了？; 他不会说 → 他不会做
trapZone.reason: 想 xiǎng and 生 shēng both end with -ng, but 想 has a clear i-glide before -ang while 生 has no i-glide and a more open central vowel. 怎么 zěnme and 人们 rénmen share the same -nme ending; the real cue is only the initial (z- with tongue behind teeth vs r- with tongue curled back). 说 shuō and 做 zuò share the -uo rhyme; the contrast is primarily tone contour (1st flat vs 4th falling) plus initial placement.

drill.zh: 你想我了，不是你生完了！
drill.py: Nǐ xiǎng wǒ le, bùshì nǐ shēng wán le!
drill.en: You miss me, not that you gave birth!

drill.zh: 他不会做，不是他不会说！
drill.py: Tā bù huì zuò, bùshì tā bù huì shuō!
drill.en: He can't do it, not that he can't speak!

characters.pronunciation: shee-ahng (keep a strong i-glide before -ang; avoid sheng-like vowel)
characters.calligraphy: TALL ║ SHORT balance. Keep 相 stable on top and 心 compact below. Focus on 心's final curved hook (卧钩) — it carries the emotional center of the character.
characters.culture: 想家 (xiǎng jiā, miss home) is one of the most emotionally loaded expressions during Spring Festival travel. 想你 (xiǎng nǐ, miss you) is one of the most direct intimate texts in modern Mandarin.
characters.etymology: Radical breakdown: 相 + 心. Early forms of 相 relate to mutual gaze or looking at each other; 心 is heart. Combined image: the heart turning toward someone not present — to think of, long for, miss.

characters.pronunciation: boo (short and firm, with a sharp fall; not soft or prolonged)
characters.calligraphy: WIDE ║ NARROW balance. Keep the top horizontal stroke steady and commanding, then let the downward structure close cleanly underneath.
characters.culture: 不 is among the highest-frequency characters in spoken Mandarin and appears constantly in daily negation: 不是, 不会, 不想. In classical and philosophical writing, forms like 不言 ('not speaking') carry rhetorical weight.
characters.etymology: Commonly taught as an ancient pictographic shape linked to 'not yet' or an unfulfilled state. Over time it grammaticalized into Mandarin's universal negator: NOT.

pairs.title: 们 vs 淇
pairs.subtitle: plural suffix vs ice-cream loan-sound
pairs.prompt: 哪个是 plural？哪个是 ice cream？
pairs.promptEn: Which one marks plural? Which one is in ice cream?

trapZone.confusion: 你回周嗎? → 你会做吗？; 他做生亡工作 → 她做什么工作？; 今天冰淇淋 → 怎么了？
trapZone.reason: 回(huí) and 会(huì) share h- onset, but huí rises with spread lips while huì falls and closes harder at the end. 周(zhōu) vs 做(zuò) swaps retroflex zh- (curled tongue) with flat z- (forward tongue). 什么(shénme) was chunked into 生亡(shēngwáng) because only the sh- cue was retained and the rest got guessed. 今天冰淇淋 for 怎么了 is a full lexical autocorrect: similar rhythm triggered your strongest familiar phrase.

characters.pronunciation: mun (sounds close to English 'men', but lighter; keep it brief and unstressed)
characters.calligraphy: NARROW ║ TALL balance. Left 亻 must stay slim and upright; 门 on the right is fuller. Keep the person radical tight so the whole character does not sprawl.
characters.culture: 们 is not used alone in modern Mandarin. It attaches to pronouns: 我们, 你们, 他们. Historical note: before the 1920s, 他 commonly covered all genders in writing; reform-era writers (including 刘半农) pushed modern distinctions like 她/它, while 们 stayed the productive plural suffix.
characters.etymology: Radical breakdown: 亻(person semantic) + 门(men phonetic). Early uses treated 门 mostly as sound; adding 亻 clarified PEOPLE as meaning. 门 alone means door, but with 亻 it becomes a plural marker for groups of people in pronouns.

characters.english: qí sound in 冰淇淋 (ice cream)
characters.pronunciation: chee (like 'cheese' without the final s), rising at the end
characters.calligraphy: WIDE ║ SHORT balance. Left 氵 uses three evenly spaced dots. Right 其 carries most width; avoid squeezing the water radical.
characters.culture: 淇 originally names the Qi River (淇河) in Henan, attested in early classics such as 《诗经》. In 冰淇淋, 淇 is mostly phonetic borrowing rather than core meaning; the phrase functions as a loan translation for 'ice cream'.
characters.etymology: Radical breakdown: 氵(water semantic) + 其(qí phonetic). Historically tied to river naming. In modern compounds like 冰淇淋, 淇 contributes sound value more than literal semantics.

pairs.title: 说 vs 游
pairs.subtitle: to speak vs to swim/roam — visual 口 trap
pairs.promptEn: Which is shuō? Which is yóu?

trapZone.confusion: 你再听我说吗 → 你在听我说吗；你做什麼工作 → 你做什么工作；说's 口 vs 游's 口 — SAME radical, different shape
trapZone.reason: 在 (zài, at/now) and 再 (zài, again) are perfect homophones — tone 4, identical consonant and vowel. Only context separates them. Visual trap: 说 has 讠(speech) + 兑 whose 口 is WIDE & SHORT (squatting 🧘), while 游 has 氵(water) + 斿 whose 口 is TALL & NARROW (stretching 🧍). Same mouth radical — completely different outfit. Your eye catches this once trained!

drill.py: Nǐ zài tīng wǒ shuō ma?

characters.english: to speak / to say / to explain
characters.tone: 1st — flat, steady (——), like holding a note
characters.pronunciation: shwō (start with English 'sh' then round lips for 'wō'. Hold flat and steady — don't let it rise or fall.)
characters.calligraphy: NARROW ║ WIDE balance. 讠is TALL & NARROW on left — the speech radical reaching up. 兑 is WIDE on right. Focus: the 口 inside 兑 is WIDE & SHORT — it's SQUATTING, not stretching! Don't make it tall.
characters.culture: 游说 (yóu shuì) = 'travel + speak' — ancient Chinese diplomats would roam from kingdom to kingdom speaking to persuade kings. This is literally 'roam and speak'. A 3000-year-old career in rhetoric! 小说 (xiǎo shuō) = novel, literally 'small talk' — classical scholars considered fiction minor speech.
characters.etymology: Radical breakdown: 讠(speech) + 兑 (joyful open mouth). 讠is simplified 言 = SPEECH. 兑 originally showed a person LAUGHING with mouth WIDE OPEN — exchanging words with JOY. Ancient story (3000 years ago): 兑 = person with wide laughing mouth. Add speech radical = speaking with pleasure → to speak, to say, to explain. What each part MEANS: 讠= words coming out, 兑 = happy/exchange (also gives sound).

characters.english: to swim / to travel / to roam
characters.pronunciation: yōw (start with 'y' like 'yes', then round lips and lift tone upward ↗. Sounds like 'yo' with a rising tail.)
characters.calligraphy: NARROW ║ WIDE balance. 氵is TALL & NARROW on left — three water drops standing tall. 斿 is WIDE on right. Focus: the 口 inside 斿 is TALL & NARROW — it's STRETCHING UP to match 斿's height! The opposite of 说's squatting 口.
characters.culture: 游山玩水 (yóu shān wán shuǐ) = 'roam mountains, play water' — the CLASSIC Chinese ideal of leisure. Every Chinese landscape painting shows someone 游-ing through nature. 游说 (yóu shuì) pairs with 说: roam AND speak together.
characters.etymology: Radical breakdown: 氵(water) + 斿 (streaming flag/banner). 氵= three water drops = WATER. 斿 was a PICTURE of a flag waving in the wind (3500 years ago) — movement, streaming, roaming. One of the oldest characters. 氵+ 斿 = moving THROUGH water → to swim, to travel, to wander. What each part MEANS: 氵= water, 斿 = moving/streaming (also gives sound yóu).

pairs.title: 哪 vs 去 (with 听)
pairs.subtitle: which/where vs to go (listening comprehension)
pairs.prompt: 哪个是 nǎ？哪个是 qù？ 你在听吗？
pairs.promptEn: Which is nǎ? Which is qù? Are you listening?

trapZone.confusion: 聽著說 → 听他说 (著 zhe vs 他 tā); 茶不會說 → 他不會做 (茶 chá vs 他 tā, 說 shuō vs 做 zuò); 早打累工作 → 哪里 (nǎlǐ → zǎo dǎ lèi, tone pattern collapse)
trapZone.reason: 哪 (nǎ, dipping tone 3↘↗) vs 早 (zǎo, dipping tone 3↘↗) — identical tone pattern! The n- vs z- initial completely shifted but listener's brain matched the TONE and misheard the whole phrase. This is why 哪里 (where) completely collapses to 早打累 (early hit tired) in fast speech — the tone pattern MATCHED. 茶 chá uses curled tongue (ch-), 他 tā uses tap (t-). 說 shuō is curled tongue, 做 zuò is flat tongue. Homophones like 聽著(listened + particle) vs 听他 exploit the identical consonant cluster but different following consonant.

drill.zh: 你在听我说吗？你去哪里？
drill.py: Nǐ zài tīng wǒ shuō ma? Nǐ qù nǎlǐ?
drill.en: Are you listening to me? Where are you going?

drill.py: Tā bù huì zuò, chá cái huì shuō.
drill.en: He can't do it, but tea can speak!

drill.py: Tīng tā shuō, bié tīng zhe nàge.
drill.en: Listen to him speak, don't keep listening to that one.

characters.tone: 3rd — dipping (down↘ then up↗), like 'naaa' with a dip in the middle
characters.pronunciation: nah (n- nasal tap, tongue taps the ridge behind teeth. Then ǎ vowel dips LOW then rises back). Start at middle, DROP LOW, rise back up — naǎ↘↗
characters.calligraphy: NARROW ║ WIDE balance. 口 (mouth) is SMALL & HIGH on the left — don't drop it low! 那 spreads WIDE on the right. The mouth is positioned high and small because you're ASKING — your mouth is open but focused upward in curiosity.
characters.culture: 哪 is NEVER used alone in speech — always pairs: 哪里 (nǎlǐ, where), 哪个 (nǎge, which one), 哪個 (nǎge, trad. — same). 哪个 is the #1 spoken question in daily life! In classical texts 那 (that one over there) evolved into 哪 (which one asking). RADICAL: 口 (mouth asking) + 那 (that one) = 'WHICH that one?!'
characters.etymology: Radical breakdown: 口 (mouth) + 那 (that). Ancient story (~3000 yrs ago): You point your hand at something and ask with your mouth: 'THAT one?!' 那 = pointing finger + city radical. 哪 = add mouth because you SPEAK it. What each part MEANS: 口 = you MUST ask out loud, 那 = that one over there, 哪 = WHICH one?!

characters.pronunciation: chyoo (q- is like 'ch' in 'church' but softer. Drop hard and fast from high to low.) Sounds like 'chew' without the 'w'. Start HIGH, drop HARD & FAST → 'chyoo!'⬇️
characters.calligraphy: TALL ║ SHORT balance. Top 大 spreads wide (shoulders open like walking). Bottom 厶 is compact (feet walking away). Don't make it too big. The 厶 bottom — it's the 'footsteps' leaving!
characters.culture: 去 is both 'to go' AND 'past/previous'. 去年 (qùnián, last year) = the year that WENT away. 去过 (qùguo, have been to) = went and came back. One character = going AND returning! 大 (person) over 厶 (private/self departing) — person leaving = GO! Ancient picture: person standing at door, steps OUT → that's 'to go'.
characters.etymology: Radical breakdown: 大 (person) over 厶 (private/self). Ancient story (~3500 yrs ago): Picture a person 大 standing at a door 囗 (enclosure = home). Person steps OUT → that's 'to go' 去! Simplified 去 keeps this image: top = person, bottom = leaving motion. MEANING: 大 = person with arms spread, 厶 = the private self departing, 去 = person + departure = GO! 🚶

characters.tone: 1st — high flat (———), like singing a held note
characters.pronunciation: ting (t- with tongue tapped hard against teeth, then -ing nasal. Hold the tone HIGH and FLAT — teeeeng 🔔 Don't let it drop!)
characters.calligraphy: NARROW ║ WIDE balance. 耳 (ear) is TALL & NARROW on the left — make it TALL, it's your ear straining to hear! 口+斤 is WIDER on the right. Focus on: 耳 must be TALL — don't squish it.
characters.culture: 听话 (tīng huà, tone 1) = 'obedient / well-behaved' — literally 'listens to words'. A good child 听妈妈的话 (listens to mom). In Qi Gong 氣功, 'listening with your heart' (用心听) means sensing energy, not just sound. Your 心 heart is the REAL ear! Traditional 聽 = 耳 (ear) + 悳 (virtue) + 直 (straight) + 心 (heart) — true listening = ear + heart together! This is why 聽 has 心 hidden inside. Mencius said: 耳不聪目不明 = 'If ears don't listen, eyes don't see' — all senses start from the 心 heart!
characters.etymology: RADICAL breakdown: 耳 (ear) + 口 + 斤. Traditional 聽 = 耳 (ear) + 悳 (virtue) + 直 (straight) + 心 (heart). Ancient story (~3000 yrs ago): Your 耳 ear catches the sound, but your 心 heart decides if it MATTERS. True listening = ear + heart together! MEANING: 耳 = physical hearing, 心 = spiritual attention, 听 = BOTH together = real listening 👂🫀

pairs.title: 在 vs 听
pairs.subtitle: at/in/existing vs to listen
pairs.prompt: 哪个是 zài？哪个是 tīng？
pairs.promptEn: Which is zài? Which is tīng?

trapZone.confusion: 你在听我说吗？→ 你那庭我说吗？ (在→那, 听→庭); 怎么了？→ 真不辣; 他不会做→他不会說; 你在哪里工作？→ 您是哪里工作？
trapZone.reason: 在 (z-, flat tongue) vs 那 (n-, tongue taps ridge) vs 是 (sh-, tongue curled back) are all 1-syllable function words — speech recognition's #1 enemy. 听 (tīng, 1st tone) and 庭 (tíng, 2nd tone) are perfect homophones — correct pronunciation, wrong character chosen by app. 你→您 is a formality default, not a pronunciation error.

drill.py: Nǐ zài tīng wǒ shuō ma?

characters.pronunciation: dzai (tongue flat, air flows free — z- is unvoiced, tongue doesn't vibrate). Drop hard and fast — dzai⬇️
characters.calligraphy: TALL ║ SHORT balance. 土 (earth/soil) on the bottom — the horizontal stroke 横 sits FLAT, it's the ground the seedling grows from. 才 (young sprout) above it reaching upward. Let the final 横 breathe — it anchors everything.
characters.culture: 在 is one of the TOP 10 most-used characters in all of Chinese — it's the glue word. 我在家 (I'm AT home). 他在这 (He IS here). Without 在 you can barely describe where anything is. A seedling sprouting on ground — 'something EXISTING at a place'.

characters.tone: 1st — high flat, like singing a held note
characters.pronunciation: tʰiŋ (tongue flat BEHIND teeth for t-, then -ing nasal ending). Hold the tone HIGH and FLAT — ting━━ — don't let it drop!
characters.calligraphy: NARROW ║ WIDE balance. 耳 (ear) radical on the LEFT — make it TALL and narrow, it's the ear standing up at attention. Right side is wider and open. The ear leans in to hear.
characters.culture: 听话 (tīng huà) = 'obedient / well-behaved' — literally 'listens to words'. A good child 听妈妈的话 (listens to mom). In the traditional character 聽, three radicals combine: 耳 (ear) + 口 (mouth) + 心 (heart) — true listening means your ear, the speaker's mouth, AND your heart are all engaged. Not just hearing — obeying through attention.

pairs.title: 他 vs 什么
pairs.subtitle: he/she/it vs what
pairs.prompt: 哪个是 tā？哪个是 shénme？
pairs.promptEn: Which is tā? Which is shénme?

trapZone.confusion: 女作什麼工作？ → heard as 你做什么工作？
trapZone.reason: 女 nǚ and 你 nǐ share tone 3 and the same n- initial. The difference is the vowel: 女 = ü (round lips), 你 = i (spread lips). In fast speech they collapse into each other. 什么 also compresses to 'sme' in natural speech.

characters.pronunciation: tah (flat, like a doctor saying 'open and say ahh')
characters.calligraphy: Left 亻 is TALL and THIN (standing person). Right 也 is WIDE with a sweeping hook. NARROW ║ WIDE — a person reaching toward someone else. Stroke 5 (the hook) — let it fling outward like you're pointing.
characters.culture: In the 1920s, 刘半农 (Liú Bànnóng) created 她 (女+也) for 'she' and 它 for 'it'. Before that, 他 was used for everyone — men and women. So in classical texts, 他 could be anyone. Context was everything.

characters.pronunciation: shun-muh (rising then flat). In fast speech compresses to 'sme' — you will NOT understand real speech without knowing this.
characters.calligraphy: 什: left 亻 NARROW, right 十 wide and crossed. 么: just 3 strokes — tiny, almost invisible. NARROW ║ TINY. Don't overwrite 么 — keep it small.
characters.culture: 什么 evolved from 甚物 ('what thing?') over centuries of spoken erosion. 么 used to be the full word 物 (thing) — a thousand years of fast speech compressed it into a neutral suffix. Every 什么 is a fossil.

pairs.title: 做 vs 说
pairs.subtitle: to do vs to say
pairs.prompt: 哪个是 zuò？哪个是 shuō？
pairs.promptEn: Which is zuò? Which is shuō?

trapZone.confusion: 我会做 → heard as 我会说
trapZone.reason: Same vowel (-uo), different initial: z- (tongue flat behind teeth) vs sh- (tongue curled back).

drill.py: Wǒ huì zuò, bù huì shuō.
drill.en: I can do it, but I can't say it.

characters.pronunciation: dzwuh (like 'dz' + 'waw', falling hard)
characters.calligraphy: Left 亻 is TALL and THIN (a standing person). Right 乍 is WIDE (arms spread). NARROW ║ WIDE. Stroke 7 (长横) is the backbone — hold it steady.
characters.culture: 做人 (zuò rén) — 'how to be a person' — is one of the most important phrases in the Confucian tradition. Not what you do, but how you live.

characters.pronunciation: sh-WOR (like 'sh' in shoe + 'wor' held flat)
characters.calligraphy: Left 言 is TALL (7 strokes — the speech radical). Right 兌 is SHORT. TALL ║ SHORT — like one person speaking, the other listening.
characters.culture: 小说 (xiǎo shuō) means 'novel' — literally 'small talk'. Classical scholars considered fiction minor speech compared to serious texts. Your favorite books were once called gossip.
